chief_complaint: heavy squeezing tightness in the middle of the chest when walking uphill in cold weather
hpi_details: 4-month history of predictable, reproducible retrosternal heaviness and squeezing tightness. The pain consistently occurs when walking uphill, carrying groceries, or hurrying to catch a train, especially on cold windy mornings. Radiates occasionally to his left inner arm and lower jaw. The discomfort forces him to stop walking, and reliably disappears completely within 3 to 5 minutes of resting. Never occurs when sitting watching TV or sleeping. No associated diaphoresis or nausea.
ideas: thinks his cholesterol buildup is narrowing the arteries supplying his heart muscle with oxygen
concerns: afraid that a complete blockage will happen soon causing a massive heart attack like his father had at age 60
expectations: wants a GTN spray to carry in his pocket and a referral for treadmill or angiogram testing
pmh: type 2 diabetes mellitus x8 years, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia
medications: metformin 1000mg BD, ramipril 10mg OD, atorvastatin 20mg OD
social_hx: non-smoker (quit 15 years ago), drinks 4 units alcohol/week, accountant, sedentary

clinical_knowledge.topic: Chronic Stable Angina evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Chronic Stable Angina is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes immediate symptom relief with sublingual Glyceryl Trinitrate (GTN) spray 400mcg PRN before exertion or during attacks (instruct to sit down before spraying, repeat after 5 mins if needed; call 999/ambulance if pain persists >15 mins after 2 sprays), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: heavy squeezing tightness in the middle of the chest when walking uphill in cold weather

Key HPI features: 4-month history of predictable, reproducible retrosternal heaviness and squeezing tightness. The pain consistently occurs when walking uphill, carrying groceries, or hurrying to catch a train, especially on cold windy mornings. Radiates occasionally to his left inner arm and lower jaw. The discomfort forces him to stop walking, and reliably disappears completely within 3 to 5 minutes of resting. Never occurs when sitting watching TV or sleeping. No associated diaphoresis or nausea.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: normal HR and BP. Cardiac auscultation: normal S1/S2 without murmurs or gallops. 12-lead resting ECG: normal sinus rhythm or minor non-specific ST/T wave changes (normal resting ECG does NOT exclude stable angina). Bloods: HbA1c, lipid profile, FBC (rule out anaemia worsening angina). Outpatient functional ischemia testing: CT Coronary Angiography (first-line in many guidelines) or exercise stress echocardiogram/treadmill test.
Relevant background/PMH: type 2 diabetes mellitus x8 years, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia
Current medications: metformin 1000mg BD, ramipril 10mg OD, atorvastatin 20mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Chronic Stable Angina.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to GERD without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Pain at rest, at lower effort than before, or lasting more than 20 minutes.
management_principles: Immediate symptom relief: prescribe sublingual Glyceryl Trinitrate (GTN) spray 400mcg PRN before exertion or during attacks (instruct to sit down before spraying, repeat after 5 mins if needed; call 999/ambulance if pain persists >15 mins after 2 sprays)
Anti-anginal prophylactic therapy: initiate beta-blocker (e.g., bisoprolol 5mg OD) or calcium channel blocker (amlodipine/diltiazem)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease

reference_soap.subjective: 61M with T2DM and HTN presents with classical exertional retrosternal squeezing chest pain radiating to left arm/jaw, promptly relieved within 5 minutes of rest.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: normal HR and BP. Cardiac auscultation: normal S1/S2 without murmurs or gallops. 12-lead resting ECG: normal sinus rhythm or minor non-specific ST/T wave changes (normal resting ECG does NOT exclude stable angina). Bloods: HbA1c, lipid profile, FBC (rule out anaemia worsening angina). Outpatient functional ischemia testing: CT Coronary Angiography (first-line in many guidelines) or exercise stress echocardiogram/treadmill test.
reference_soap.assessment: Chronic Stable Angina Pectoris secondary to coronary artery disease. DDx: unstable angina / ACS (differentiated by lack of rest pain, accelerating frequency, or prolonged duration >20 mins), gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, musculoskeletal chest pain, aortic stenosis.
reference_soap.plan: Immediate symptom relief: prescribe sublingual Glyceryl Trinitrate (GTN) spray 400mcg PRN before exertion or during attacks (instruct to sit down before spraying, repeat after 5 mins if needed; call 999/ambulance if pain persists >15 mins after 2 sprays). Anti-anginal prophylactic therapy: initiate beta-blocker (e.g., bisoprolol 5mg OD) or calcium channel blocker (amlodipine/diltiazem). Secondary cardiovascular prevention: up-titrate atorvastatin to 80mg OD, add aspirin 75mg OD. Refer to cardiology for CT coronary angiography or rapid-access chest pain clinic.

learning_objectives: Apply the three clinical characteristics of typical stable angina: constricting anterior chest pain, provoked by exertion, and relieved promptly by rest/GTN within 5 minutes
Instruct the patient on exact safety rules for sublingual GTN spray usage and when to activate emergency services
Formulate dual-track management of stable CAD: symptomatic anti-anginal prophylaxis (beta-blocker) plus secondary prevention (statin/aspirin)
Differentiate chronic stable angina from unstable coronary syndromes requiring immediate emergency admission

teaching.one_liner: Fixed coronary narrowing: predictable chest tightness at a predictable level of effort, relieved by rest within minutes.
red_flags: Pain at rest, at lower effort than before, or lasting more than 20 minutes

must_ask.say: Does it come on when you walk uphill or climb stairs, and settle when you rest?
How long does it take to settle once you stop?
Is it coming on with less effort than it used to?
How would you describe it — sharp, crushing, burning, tight?

must_ask.objective: Site and radiation of the pain
must_ask.say: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move anywhere else?
Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol, and do you smoke?

history.answer: Whenever I walk uphill or carry heavy groceries, especially in this cold weather, I get a heavy squeezing tightness right in the middle of my chest.
This started about four months ago, and it happens whenever I walk uphill, carry shopping bags, or hurry to catch a train on cold, windy mornings.
It is right in the center of my chest, deep behind my breastbone, and it covers a wide area rather than one spot I can point to with a finger.
It feels like a heavy squeezing tightness or a heavy weight pressing down on my chest, not sharp or stabbing at all.
Sometimes the tight ache spreads down into the inside of my left arm and up along my lower jaw.
Once I stop walking and rest, the feeling reliably goes away completely within three to five minutes.
When it peaks, I would rate the discomfort at about a 5 or 6 out of 10, enough that it forces me to stop walking right away.
Exertion always brings it on, and stopping to rest reliably takes it away completely every single time.
It has stayed very predictable and stable over these four months, coming on at about the same amount of effort without getting more frequent or severe.
No, I never get this tightness when I am sitting on the couch watching television or resting in bed at night.
No, taking a deep breath, coughing, or moving around does not change the tightness at all.
No, pressing on my chest or ribs does not hurt and does not bring on that tight feeling.
No, it does not happen after meals, lying flat does not trigger it, and I have no acid reflux, sour taste, or trouble swallowing.
No, I haven't broken out into cold sweats and I don't feel sick to my stomach when the pain happens.
I get a little out of breath just from the physical effort, but I don't have severe breathlessness, dizziness, or fainting.
No, I have had no fever, chills, cough, or phlegm.
No, I haven't had a cold, the flu, or any viral illness recently.
No, neither leg is swollen or painful, and I haven't been on any long flights or had surgery recently.
No, there are no rashes, sores, or blisters on my chest or back.
I feel anxious about my heart, but I don't have sudden panic attacks, trembling, or tingling in my hands.
No, I haven't had any injuries or hits to my chest, and I haven't done any heavy weightlifting.
I had a normal routine checkup ECG a couple of years ago, but I have never had an angiogram, stress test, or stents placed.
I suspect cholesterol buildup is narrowing the arteries that supply blood and oxygen to my heart muscle.
I am terrified that one of the arteries will block completely and trigger a fatal heart attack like my father had at age sixty.
I was hoping to get a prescription for that under-the-tongue nitro spray to keep with me, and a referral for a treadmill test or angiogram.
I have had type 2 diabetes for eight years, along with high blood pressure and high cholesterol.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never stayed overnight in a hospital.
I take metformin 1000 milligrams twice a day, ramipril 10 milligrams once a day, and atorvastatin 20 milligrams once a day, with no other supplements.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I used to smoke, but I quit completely fifteen years ago and haven't touched a cigarette since.
I drink about four units of alcohol a week, usually just a couple of beers over the weekend.
I work as an accountant, so I sit at a desk most of the day, and I live with my wife in a two-story house.
My father died suddenly of a massive heart attack when he was sixty years old, and my mother had diabetes in her later years.

exam.finding: Alert and comfortable at rest in no acute distress, with normal skin colour and no diaphoresis.
Blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 36.6°C.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are non-icteric.
Jugular venous pressure is normal, without visible jugular venous distension.
No visible chest wall lesions or deformity, and palpation of the ribs and chondrosternal joints does not elicit tenderness or reproduce the chest pain.
Resonant percussion notes throughout both lung fields.
Normal vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or pleural friction rubs.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds, and no murmurs, gallops, or pericardial friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender without palpable masses, organomegaly, or epigastric discomfort.
No pitting edema in either lower extremity.
Calves are symmetric, non-tender, and without warmth, swelling, or cords.
